title: India Targets Back-End Semiconductor and Analog Chips as Global Supply Chains Fragment
excerpt: With billions in government incentives and facilities from Micron, Tata, and CG Power coming online, India is carving out a strategic niche in chip assembly, testing, and specialized analog production.
body:
• India is positioning itself as a global hub for back-end semiconductor operations (OSAT, assembly, testing) and specialized analog chip production, rather than competing in leading-edge logic fabrication.
  • The India Semiconductor Mission, initially funded at $9.2 billion, has attracted over $90 billion in cumulative private investment, with facilities from Micron, Tata Electronics, and CG Power now in various stages of production.
  • US-India trade policy adjustments have lowered import tariffs on Indian-made electronics to 18%, compared with 34%+ on Chinese components — drawing companies like Apple to integrate Indian-packaged chips.
  • India's semiconductor component market is projected to reach $300 billion by 2026, driven by demand from automotive, industrial, and AI sectors.

A Strategic Bet on the Back End

As geopolitical tensions fracture global semiconductor supply chains, India is making a deliberate strategic choice: rather than chasing the capital-prohibitive race for leading-edge logic chips, the country is building itself into a critical hub for back-end operations and specialized analog production.

https://x.com/moneycontrolcom/status/2094394817820385760

According to PwC analysis, regions are now specializing rather than competing across all semiconductor segments. India's focus on OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test), analog chips, and microcontrollers positions it in sectors essential for the automotive and industrial markets — segments that constitute the overwhelming majority of the 1.05 trillion chips sold globally each year, according to DQ India.

Prof. Dr. Milind Pande of MIT-WPU notes that this alignment leverages India's established design talent pool and offers "a realistic entry point into the advanced manufacturing sector, fitting a niche that is essential to the broader global ecosystem."

Billions in Investment Coming Online

The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), launched in December 2021 with an initial outlay of approximately $9.2 billion, has served as the central policy engine. The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme offers up to 50% of project costs for fabs and ATMP facilities, potentially reaching 75% with state-level subsidies, according to Cornell Business.

Several major facilities are now operational or nearing completion. Micron Technology's $2.75 billion facility in Sanand, Gujarat — India's first major semiconductor plant — is producing high-density DRAM and NAND flash memory chips. Tata Electronics is constructing an $11 billion mega-fab in Dholera in partnership with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp, targeting 28nm and 55nm logic chips for automotive and IoT applications.

In Assam, a Tata OSAT facility with a projected capacity of 48 million chips per day is nearing commissioning, specializing in advanced packaging techniques. And CG Power, in a joint venture with Japan's Renesas Electronics and Thailand's Stars Microelectronics, has entered pilot production for specialized power and analog chips at a $918 million facility in Gujarat.

Trade Policy Tailwinds

Geopolitical realignment is working in India's favor. Recent US-India trade policy adjustments have lowered import tariffs on Indian-made electronics to 18% — significantly below the 34%-plus often levied on Chinese components. Apple has already begun integrating Indian-packaged memory and power management chips into its latest product lines, de-risking its hardware supply chain from single-region dependence.

Major global firms have made substantial commitments: Applied Materials is investing $400 million in an engineering center, Lam Research has pledged $25 million for a semiconductor training lab to train 60,000 Indian engineers, and AMD is expanding R&D operations with a $400 million investment.

The Competitive Challenge

India's path is not without obstacles. Pricing pressure from Chinese foundries — where costs are already more than 10% lower — remains a persistent concern, according to Computer Weekly. Mature-node plants are cheaper to set up and quicker to pay back, but that also means easier entry for rivals.

Water intensity, high energy requirements for wafer fabrication, and the need for green energy corridors specifically for semiconductor parks are additional hurdles the government is actively addressing.

Kanishka Chauhan, senior principal analyst at Gartner, argues that India should adopt a "high-mix, low-volume model" to avoid flooding the market with commoditized chips. The real value, he adds, lies in establishing India as a hub for supply chain resilience: "With rising geopolitical tensions, India's proactive efforts to de-risk supply chains will make it more attractive to global industries."

What to Watch

The government has already pivoted to ISM 2.0, shifting focus from anchoring large fabs to building the ancillary ecosystem — including semiconductor equipment manufacturing and sovereign chip design IP. Experts predict India could account for nearly 10% of the global semiconductor assembly and testing market by 2028.

The next key milestone is the rollout of Tata's first 28nm chips, expected in late 2026, which would mark a significant leap in domestic fabrication capability.
